output:
Kelechi,

You said if I was serious, I should put it in writing. So here you go: an actual letter, posted to Croydon like it’s 1998. You can read it on the train and pretend you’re not smiling.

I’m serious about the maths teaching idea. Not “quit your job tomorrow and follow your dreams” serious. You know I’d never talk to you like that. I mean: serious enough to think you should at least come and see what the route looks like before you dismiss it.

You’ve been at the same quantity-surveying firm for nine years, and every time we talk about work you say it’s the same spreadsheet in a different outfit. I know you’re good at it. That’s almost the irritating part: you’re very capable of doing a job that seems to leave you bored to death. And on your last birthday, you said you wanted to do something that mattered before 40. I remembered. Annoying, I know.

Also, I haven’t forgotten that A in Further Maths. Or the fact that half of Moremi seemed to end up getting tutored by you before exams. You never made anyone feel stupid for not getting it straight away; you’d just explain it another way until it clicked. Remember my nephew and the fractions at Christmas? You put jollof rice portions on plates, and he still talks about it. I’m pretty sure you accidentally taught him more than fractions that day. He knows not to mess with the person dividing the rice.

I’m not saying teaching is easy, or that being good at explaining maths automatically makes you a great teacher. There’s a lot to learn, and some days are properly hard. I cried in the car park twice during my first term in 2019. I’m not hiding that from you. The marking can feel endless, and some days behaviour is wahala. You’ll plan something clever and a class will respond as if you’ve asked them to inspect a spreadsheet for fun. It can be exhausting.

But it does get better. You find your feet, you learn what works, and every so often you get a moment that makes all the difficult bits feel worth it. Last month, one of my Year 11s, Damola, finally got simultaneous equations after three weeks of going round in circles. He looked at the page and shouted, “Is that all??” The whole class clapped. No spreadsheet has ever got that reaction, has it?

And I’m not suggesting this because our school needs staff, even though it really does. We’ve had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups since September, and there are about 1,100 kids here. I know what it’s like when pupils need someone consistent who can explain things without making them feel small. You’d be patient with them. You’re funny without trying too hard. They’d like you, though I reserve the right to deny saying that if they become insufferable about it.

There’s a salaried training route: you’re paid while you train, it takes a year, and the start date is September 2027. Yes, there’d be a pay drop in the first year. I’m not going to pretend that’s nothing. But there are holidays, a pension, and the pay goes up. You’d need to look at the details and decide whether the numbers work for you. I’m not asking you to hand in your notice based on one letter from your old friend.

And before you say you’re too old: you’re 34, not a Victorian ghost. A woman in my department started at 41. You have plenty of time to make a change if you decide you want one. Nine years of quantity surveying is not a life sentence, even if your spreadsheets seem committed to the relationship.

So here is the actual ask: come with me to the open evening on **Thursday 19 November 2026 at 6pm**, at the training partnership in Lewisham. Applications for next September open soon, so it’s a good time to find out what the training involves, ask awkward questions about the money, and hear the honest version from people who know the route. You don’t have to sign anything. You don’t have to decide anything. You can come, listen, and then tell me you hated it over food afterwards.

I’ll go with you. I promise not to turn it into a lecture or say “this is your calling” while pointing dramatically at a whiteboard. I’m asking because I know you, and I think you might be good at this. More than that, I think it could be the kind of work you said you wanted before 40: hard, sometimes maddening, but useful in a way you can actually see.

Come to the evening. That’s all. One train ride, one look around, and no commitment beyond letting me buy you something afterwards.

Your friend,

[Your name]
